derivations.claim: The interval $I$ is one of the four open forms of [F1], hence an open subset of $\mathbb R$; fix a real $\varepsilon>0$ with $N_\varepsilon(0)\subseteq I$. By [F2] the punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_\varepsilon(0)$ is a nonempty subset of $N_\varepsilon(0)\subseteq I$, so $I$ contains $0$ and at least one further point and is therefore nondegenerate; by [F3] every point of $I$ is a limit point of $I$, that is, by [F4], $N^{*}_\eta(\theta)\cap I\ne\varnothing$ for every $\theta\in I$ and every real $\eta>0$.

The function $F$ is totally differentiable at $p:=\gamma(\theta)=\theta_0+\theta u$, and $D_uF(p)=\langle\nabla F(p),u\rangle$: as $F$ is of class $C^1$, each first partial derivative $\partial_jF$ exists and is continuous on the open set $U$ by [F16], so [F14] gives total differentiability of $F$ at $p\in U$, and [F17] gives $D_uF(p)=\langle\nabla F(p),u\rangle$.

The path $\gamma:I\to U$ is continuous at every $\theta'\in I$: given a real $\varepsilon>0$ take $\delta:=\varepsilon$; for $\theta''\in I$ with $|\theta''-\theta'|<\delta$ one has $d_2\bigl(\gamma(\theta''),\gamma(\theta')\bigr)=\lVert\gamma(\theta'')-\gamma(\theta')\rVert_2=\lVert(\theta''-\theta')u\rVert_2=|\theta''-\theta'|\,\lVert u\rVert_2=|\theta''-\theta'|<\varepsilon$, by [F19], the homogeneity axiom (N2) of [F22] and $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$; this is continuity in the metric sense of [F21].

The configuration displacement has Euclidean length $\lVert\gamma(\theta)-\theta_0\rVert_2=\lVert\theta u\rVert_2=|\theta|\,\lVert u\rVert_2=|\theta|$, by the Euclidean norm of [F19], the homogeneity axiom (N2) of [F22] and $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$.

For every $\theta\in I$ the components of the path satisfy $\gamma_j(\theta+t)=\gamma_j(\theta)+tu_j$ for every real $t$ with $\theta+t\in I$, since $\gamma_j(\theta+t)=(\theta_0)_j+(\theta+t)u_j=(\theta_0)_j+\theta u_j+tu_j=\gamma_j(\theta)+tu_j$ by field arithmetic; on $I$ the functions $1_I:=p_0|_I$, constantly $1$, and $\mathrm{id}_I:=p_1|_I$, the identity, are differentiable at $\theta$ with derivatives $0$ and $1$, because the power functions $p_0$ and $p_1$ have those derivatives at every real by [F7] and $\theta$ is a limit point of $I$ by step 1.1, so [F6] restricts; since $\gamma_j=(\theta_0)_j\cdot1_I+u_j\cdot\mathrm{id}_I$ on $I$, the sum and scalar rules of [F8] give that $\gamma_j$ is differentiable at $\theta$ with $\gamma_j'(\theta)=(\theta_0)_j\cdot0+u_j\cdot1=u_j$.

Each composite $\partial_jF\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous: for open $V\subseteq\mathbb R$ the preimage $(\partial_jF\circ\gamma)^{-1}[V]$ is, by [F23], the preimage $\gamma^{-1}\bigl[\partial_jF^{-1}[V]\bigr]$; the set $\partial_jF^{-1}[V]$ is open in the domain $U$ of the continuous $\partial_jF$ by the choice-free equivalence (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(b) of [F21], and its preimage under the continuous $\gamma$ is therefore open in $I$; the same equivalence then gives continuity of $\partial_jF\circ\gamma$ on $I$.

For every $\theta\in I$ the partial derivative of $\gamma_j$ in the direction $e_0=1$ equals its ordinary derivative, so $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)=u_j$: by [F9] the directional derivative $D_{e_0}\gamma_j(\theta)$ is the limit at $0$ of $t\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(\theta+t)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/t$, while by [F5] the derivative $\gamma_j'(\theta)=u_j$ of step 2.1 is the limit at $\theta$ of $x\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/(x-\theta)$; the substitution $x=\theta+t$ carries one punctured domain bijectively onto the other and the two $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ conditions of [F10] are the same condition, so $D_{e_0}\gamma_j(\theta)=\gamma_j'(\theta)=u_j$.

For every $\theta\in I$ the partial derivative of the path is the vector $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$: the quotient $q_\theta(t):=\bigl(\gamma(\theta+t)-\gamma(\theta)\bigr)/t$ on its domain $\{\,t:t\ne0,\ \theta+t\in I\,\}$ is identically $u$ by the component identity in step 2.1, so its limit exists and defines $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)$ by [F9], the $j$-th component of $q_\theta$ is $t\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(\theta+t)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/t$ with limit $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)$, and step 3.1 gives $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)=u_j$; by the componentwise limit criterion [F11] the $j$-th coordinate of $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)$ equals $u_j$ for every $j<n$, and two vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ with equal coordinates are equal by [F19], so $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$.

The only partial derivative of $\gamma$ is the constant $\partial_0\gamma\equiv u$ on $I$ by step 4.1 applied at every $\theta\in I$, and it is continuous at $\theta$: given a real $\varepsilon>0$, every $\delta>0$ serves for the continuity condition of [F12], because $\lVert\partial_0\gamma(\theta')-\partial_0\gamma(\theta)\rVert_2=\lVert u-u\rVert_2=0<\varepsilon$ for every $\theta'\in I$.

The path $\gamma$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$ with $D\gamma(\theta)(1)=u$: the partial derivative $\partial_0\gamma$ exists on the neighbourhood $I$ of $\theta$ in the open domain $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and is continuous at $\theta$ by step 5.1, so $D\gamma(\theta)$ exists by [F14]; moreover $D\gamma(\theta)(1)=D\gamma(\theta)(e_0)=\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$ by [F15] and step 4.1.

The composite $g:=F\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at every $\theta\in I$ with $Dg(\theta)=DF(\gamma(\theta))\circ D\gamma(\theta)$ by the chain rule [F20], applied to the totally differentiable $\gamma$ of step 6.1 and $F$ of step 1.2; consequently $g'(\theta)=Dg(\theta)(1)=DF(\gamma(\theta))\bigl(D\gamma(\theta)(1)\bigr)=DF(\gamma(\theta))(u)=D_uF(\gamma(\theta))=\langle\nabla F(\gamma(\theta)),u\rangle\ge m$ for every $\theta\in I$, where the first equality identifies the ordinary derivative with the total derivative applied to $1$ (the limits of [F9] and [F5] coincide as in step 3.1) and the remaining equalities are step 6.1, [F15] and step 1.2.

The derivative $g'$ is continuous on $I$: on $I$ one has $g'(\theta)=\sum_{j<n}u_j\,(\partial_jF\circ\gamma)(\theta)$ by step 7.1, the gradient definition [F18] and the inner product of [F19]; the composites are continuous by step 2.2, the dictionary of [F21] transfers this to the real reading, and finite sums and scalar multiples of functions continuous at each point of $I$ are continuous there by the algebra clause of [F21]; in particular $g'$ is continuous on $I$ in the sense required by [F24].

The value of $g$ at the centre is $g(0)=F(\theta_0+0\cdot u)=F(\theta_0)=0$, and $I$ has at least two elements with $0\in I$ by step 1.1; the function $g:I\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ with continuous derivative by steps 7.1 and 8.1, and $g'\ge m>0$ on $I$ by step 7.1.

The bounded-error model comparison [F24] now applies to $g$ on $I$ with centre $\theta_0:=0$ and the recorded scalar $\hat y$, $s$, $\delta$ of the statement, because a model value $y=g(\theta)=F(\theta_0+\theta u)$ at the candidate $\theta\in I$ is exactly the quantity the calibration bound constrains; its conclusion is $|\theta-0|\le(s+\delta)/m$, that is $|\theta|\le(s+\delta)/m$, and the equivalent contrapositive form says that a proposed $\theta$ violating this bound is incompatible with the two stated bounds; with the displacement identity of step 1.4 the statement is proved.

derivations.claim: For $F(\theta)=m\theta$ the theorem's hypotheses are met at $n=1$, $U=\mathbb R$, $\theta_0=0$, $u=1$, $I=\mathbb R$ with lower bound $m$: $\mathbb R$ is an open interval containing $0$ and is open in itself [F2], the identity on $\mathbb R$ is differentiable everywhere with derivative $1$ [F4], so the scalar multiple $F=m\,p_1$ is differentiable everywhere with $F'(\theta)=m\cdot1=m$ at every real, a limit point of the domain [F3, F5]; for $\varepsilon>0$, taking $r=\varepsilon/m>0$ gives $|F(x)-F(c)|=m|x-c|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|x-c|<r$, so $F$ is continuous; the derivative function is the constant $m$, whose differences are zero, hence it too is continuous, so $F$ is of class $C^1$ [F10]; $F(0)=0$; the only partial derivative is $\partial_0F(\theta)=D_1F(\theta)=F'(\theta)=m$ [F6], so $\nabla F(\theta)=(m)$ [F7] and $\langle\nabla F(\theta),1\rangle=m\cdot1=m\ge m$ [F8]; and $\lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert(1)\rVert_2=1$ [F8].

With the recorded $\hat y=0$, $s=0$ and $y=F(\theta)=m\theta$ the two bounds read $0\le0$ and $|m\theta|\le\delta$; since $|m\theta|=m\,|\theta|$ and $m>0$, the inequality $|m\theta|\le\delta$ is equivalent to $|\theta|\le\delta/m$ [F9]. By the theorem [F1] every compatible $\theta$ satisfies $|\theta|\le(s+\delta)/m=\delta/m$, so the compatible set is exactly the set of $\theta$ with $|\theta|\le\delta/m$; at $\theta=\pm\delta/m$ one has $|m\theta|=m\,(\delta/m)=\delta$, so these candidates are compatible and the bound is attained, and no smaller constant can replace $\delta/m$ for this instance; if $\delta=0$ then $|m\theta|=0$ forces $\theta=0$, the only compatible candidate [F9].

For $F\equiv0$ and $m=0$ the function is the scalar multiple $0\cdot p_1$, differentiable everywhere with derivative $0$ [F4, F5], so $\partial_0F(\theta)=0$ and $\nabla F(\theta)=(0)$ [F6, F7], whence $\langle\nabla F(\theta),1\rangle=0$; this is not $\ge m$ for any $m>0$, so the theorem's hypothesis fails and the theorem supplies no bound. Nevertheless $y=F(\theta)=0=\hat y$ for every real $\theta$, so $|y-\hat y|=0\le\delta$ and $|\hat y|=0\le s$ hold for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$: with the same indicator and the same two bounds every real $\theta$ is compatible, and no finite bound $|\theta|\le C$ follows from those data alone [F9].
